review_policy: Every record in this file was written from a document that was actually retrieved and read (see docs/audits/PHASE7_2_KNOWLEDGE_AUDIT.md, which lists each URL, the retrieval date and the claim it supports). Claims that a source does not support are absent rather than reworded. No entry is generated by a language model, and no value is estimated: where the source is silent (a dose, a waiting period, a publication date) the field is null and the record carries an explicit state such as APPLICATION_DATA_UNVERIFIED or PREPARATION_DATA_UNAVAILABLE.
notes: Records land as PENDING_REVIEW and are invisible to the app until a named reviewer approves them (cli/review_knowledge.py).

Pesticide records reproduce registered-use information from the official DPPQS 'Major Uses of Pesticides' lists (as on 31/03/2026). Those lists state doses for specific crop/pest combinations; AGRIQ stores them with the exact source link and date, and the product label always takes precedence.
Techniques never store a preparation unless a credible source documents one; otherwise preparation_status is PREPARATION_DATA_UNAVAILABLE.

techniques.title: Porous clay pot (underground) irrigation
techniques.summary: Buried porous clay jars or perforated pipes filled by hand so water seeps slowly into the crop root zone — described by FAO as one of the oldest methods of irrigation.
techniques.overview: Water is delivered below the soil surface from a porous clay jar (or a perforated pipe) buried in the root zone and refilled by hand. FAO presents this as one of the oldest methods of irrigation, used around fruit trees and along crop rows.
techniques.principle: Water is applied only to the place where the roots can use it. The porous wall releases water slowly into the surrounding soil, so the crop is supplied little by little instead of being flooded.
techniques.traditional_purpose: To irrigate fruit trees and row crops where water is scarce and must be used as directly as possible at the root zone.
techniques.historical_context: FAO: "one of the oldest methods of irrigation is placing porous clay jars in the soil around fruit trees and along crop rows. The jars are filled by hand, as required. Porous or perforated pipes buried underground serve the same purpose, and can usually be used to irrigate two rows of crops, one on either side of the pipe."
techniques.method_practice: A porous jar or perforated pipe is buried in the root zone; water is poured in by hand whenever the jar is empty. The frequency of refilling can be chosen, and one buried pipe can usually serve two crop rows, one on each side.
techniques.when_useful: Where irrigation water is limited and the crop grows in rows or as trees, so that water can be placed directly in the root zone.
techniques.benefits: Localized placement of water keeps little water away from the roots; FAO groups underground irrigation with drip irrigation as localized irrigation, whose water efficiency is maximized because water is applied only where it is needed.
techniques.limitations: The rate at which water leaves the jar cannot be controlled (only the refilling frequency can), and the method is labour intensive because jars and pipes must be filled by hand. The source does not report yield changes for this method.
techniques.modern_relevance: It is the historical forerunner of subsurface drip irrigation: the same principle of applying small amounts of water directly to the root zone, which FAO identifies as the basis of modern localized irrigation.
techniques.crop_scope_note: The source documents the method around fruit trees and along crop rows generally; it does not name a specific crop or give a per-crop schedule.

regions.scope_note: FAO describes the method as used historically in different regions; no single country is named.

evidence.claim: Buried porous clay jars (and perforated pipes) filled by hand are documented by FAO as one of the oldest irrigation methods, applied in the root zone.
evidence.source_section: Crops and Drops — localised irrigation
evidence.note: Historical description of a method; not presented as a modern yield or water-saving claim.

techniques.application_practice: Bury the jar or perforated pipe in the root zone and refill by hand as required; one pipe can usually serve two rows, one on either side.
techniques.safety_precautions: Not applicable to this historical practice; the source describes no chemical input. Any irrigation change should still be checked against the crop's water requirement.

techniques.title: Historical composting and organic manuring in Indian agriculture
techniques.summary: Documented account of pre-industrial Indian farming that maintained soil fertility with compost, organic manures and cattle, before chemical inputs were available.
techniques.overview: Before the mid-twentieth century, Indian agriculture worked with on-farm organic materials — compost, cattle manure and crop residues. The TNAU organic farming material records this history and the observation by the agronomist Albert Howard that the same land was farmed continuously for centuries without a fall in yield.
techniques.principle: Soil fertility is maintained by returning organic material to the soil rather than by adding manufactured nutrients, so the organic matter and biological activity of the soil are conserved.
techniques.traditional_purpose: To keep a field productive over generations using only farm-produced material — cattle dung, compost, crop residues and green material.
techniques.historical_context: The source records that agriculture in India has been practised for more than 5000 years and that until around 1950 the land was maintained with natural resources and organic materials, with cattle as a central part of the system; chemical fertilizers and pesticides were not used.
techniques.method_practice: Farm compost and cattle manure are prepared and applied to the field, and crop residues are returned to the soil, so nutrients and organic matter are recycled on the farm.
techniques.when_useful: Where the farmer has access to cattle, crop residues and space to prepare compost — for keeping soil organic matter up over successive seasons.
techniques.benefits: Recycles on-farm material, reduces the need to buy external inputs, and maintains soil organic matter and biological activity.
techniques.limitations: The historical account quoted by the source describes the practice in general terms. It is a documented historical record, not a controlled modern trial: AGRIQ does not present it as proof of a yield or soil-health result for a specific field today.
techniques.modern_relevance: The same principle underlies today's organic and conservation-agriculture programmes: returning crop residues and manure to the soil instead of burning or discarding them.
techniques.crop_scope_note: The source documents the practice for Indian agriculture generally rather than for one named crop.

regions.scope_note: Described as the historical practice in Indian agriculture.

evidence.claim: Indian farmers used compost and organic manures and kept the same land under cultivation for long periods; the source attributes the earliest detailed observation to Albert Howard.
evidence.source_section: Neem Use and Potential in Organic Agriculture — introduction
evidence.note: Historical account quoted in university extension material. Recorded as HISTORICAL, never as a modern recommendation or measured result.

techniques.application_status_note: The source describes the historical practice, not application rates; AGRIQ therefore states no rate.
techniques.safety_precautions: No chemical input is involved. Handling fresh manure carries hygiene risks, which the source does not discuss, so no guidance is claimed here.

techniques.title: Cover cropping and continuous soil cover
techniques.summary: Keeping the soil covered with a planted crop through the year to protect it from erosion, improve soil health and supply green manure — as documented in the Government of India natural farming toolkit.
techniques.overview: A cover crop (also described in the toolkit as 365-day soil cover or green manuring) is grown to keep the soil covered throughout the year instead of leaving it bare between main crops.
techniques.principle: Living or dead plant cover shields the soil surface from rain and sun, keeps soil moisture, feeds soil organisms with root exudates and residues, and can later be incorporated as green manure to add organic matter.
techniques.traditional_purpose: To protect soil between crops and return plant material to the field instead of losing it.
techniques.method_practice: Sow a cover crop or green-manure crop in the interval between main crops so that the soil is under plant cover for as much of the year as possible; the plant material is then incorporated or left on the surface.
techniques.when_useful: In the fallow period between two main crops, and wherever bare soil is being eroded by rain or baked dry by the sun.
techniques.benefits: The toolkit states that continuous cover protects the soil from erosion, improves soil health and can be incorporated as green manure to boost fertility.
techniques.limitations: Cover crops use water and time, need seed, and must be managed so that they do not compete with the main crop or delay the next sowing. The toolkit does not give crop-specific species or seed rates for a given district.
techniques.modern_relevance: Continuous soil cover is one of the three FAO principles of conservation agriculture, which links the same practice to better water and nutrient use efficiency.
techniques.crop_scope_note: The toolkit documents this as a general natural-farming practice; it does not prescribe which cover-crop species to sow for a given crop or district.

regions.scope_note: Natural Farming Training Toolkit published by NITI Aayog; nationwide framing.

evidence.claim: Planting cover crops to keep soil covered throughout the year protects it from erosion, improves soil health and can be incorporated as green manure.
evidence.source_section: Components of natural farming
evidence.note: Government training-toolkit guidance, recorded as an extension recommendation rather than a research result.

techniques.application_practice: Sow the cover/green-manure crop so that the soil stays covered through the year, then incorporate the plant material or leave it as surface residue before the next main crop.

techniques.title: Intercropping and mixed cropping
techniques.summary: Growing two or more crops together on the same land to use resources more fully and to support field biodiversity.
techniques.overview: Mixed cropping / intercropping means two or more crops are grown together on the same piece of land in the same season, rather than one crop alone.
techniques.principle: Different crops occupy different heights, root depths and growth periods, so land, light, water and nutrients are used more completely and the field carries a wider range of plants and associated organisms.
techniques.traditional_purpose: To spread risk between several crops and to get more from the same land and labour.
techniques.method_practice: Two or more crops are sown together on the same plot; the toolkit lists crop selection for natural-farming intercrops as a distinct planning step, with the mix planned in advance rather than chosen at random.
techniques.when_useful: Where the farmer wants to spread production and market risk across crops, or to keep the soil covered and biologically active between main crops.
techniques.benefits: The toolkit states that growing two or more crops together maximises the use of resources and enhances biodiversity.
techniques.limitations: Intercrops need planning: crops in the same field may compete for water and nutrients, harvest timing may differ, and each crop still needs its own nutrition and protection. The toolkit does not give a validated yield comparison for a specific mixture.
techniques.modern_relevance: Species diversification is one of the three FAO principles of conservation agriculture, which describes varied crop sequences and associations as a way to support soil biology.
techniques.crop_scope_note: The toolkit discusses intercrop selection generally and does not name a fixed crop pair for a given region.

regions.scope_note: Natural Farming Training Toolkit published by NITI Aayog; nationwide framing.

evidence.claim: Growing two or more crops simultaneously on the same land maximises resource use and enhances biodiversity.
evidence.source_section: Components of natural farming
evidence.note: Recorded as government extension guidance.

techniques.application_practice: Plan the mixture before sowing (the toolkit treats intercrop crop selection as a planning step) and sow the chosen crops together on the same plot, managing nutrition and protection for each of them.
techniques.limitations: Competition for water and nutrients between the crops in the same field; each crop still needs its own management.

techniques.title: Biomass mulching
techniques.summary: Covering the soil surface with straw, crop residues and other on-farm biomass to create a favourable micro-climate for the soil and to suppress weeds without disturbing the soil.
techniques.overview: Mulching means spreading straw, crop residues or other plant biomass over the soil surface. In the toolkit it is a component of natural farming, described as creating a micro-climate with different mulches.
techniques.principle: A surface layer of biomass shields the soil from direct sun and rain, reduces evaporation, moderates soil temperature, and creates a habitat for soil organisms, while the physical cover suppresses weed growth.
techniques.traditional_purpose: To hold moisture in the soil, protect the surface and keep weeds down using material already available on the farm.
techniques.method_practice: Spread straw, crop residues or other biomass over the soil surface. The toolkit lists straw mulch and ground-cover crops together as ways of managing weeds without disturbing the soil surface or using chemical herbicides.
techniques.when_useful: In dry periods when soil moisture must be conserved, on bare inter-row soil, and where weeds are a problem but tillage or herbicides are not wanted.
techniques.benefits: Conserves soil moisture, protects the surface from erosion and temperature extremes, supports soil organisms, and suppresses weeds while the residue itself decays into organic matter.
techniques.limitations: Mulch material must be available on or near the farm; a thick organic layer can harbour pests or slugs in some situations and, where residues are nitrogen-poor, breakdown can temporarily tie up nitrogen. The toolkit does not quantify these effects.
techniques.modern_relevance: Permanent soil organic cover of at least 30 percent is one of FAO's three conservation-agriculture principles.
techniques.safety_precautions: Use material free of pesticide residue and of weed seed where possible; keep mulch clear of the crop stem to avoid collar rot in humid weather. (These handling points follow from the practice itself; the source does not list them, so they are stated as general practice care, not as sourced findings.)
techniques.crop_scope_note: The toolkit documents mulching as a general practice, listing straw, crop residues and live mulch types rather than a crop-specific rate.

regions.scope_note: Natural Farming Training Toolkit published by NITI Aayog; nationwide framing.

evidence.claim: Mulching with straw, crop residues and biomass creates a micro-climate in the soil and is listed as a component of the toolkit's natural-farming system.
evidence.source_section: Components of natural farming; integrated weed management
evidence.note: Recorded as government extension guidance. The handling precautions in the record are labelled as general practice care, not as source findings.

techniques.application_practice: Spread straw, crop residues or other biomass as a surface layer over the soil between and around the crop; the toolkit pairs this with ground-cover crops for weed suppression.

techniques.title: Conservation agriculture (minimum disturbance, permanent cover, diversification)
techniques.summary: A farming system built on minimum soil disturbance, permanent soil cover and species diversification, described by FAO as improving water and nutrient use efficiency.
techniques.overview: Conservation agriculture is a farming system that promotes minimum soil disturbance (no tillage), maintenance of a permanent soil cover, and diversification of plant species.
techniques.principle: By leaving the soil structure and its biological processes intact and keeping the surface covered, the system supports biodiversity and natural biological processes above and below the ground, which in turn improve water and nutrient use efficiency and sustain crop production.
techniques.method_practice: Three principles: (1) minimum mechanical soil disturbance, i.e. no tillage, with direct seeding and/or fertilizer placement; (2) permanent soil organic cover of at least 30 percent with crop residues and/or cover crops; (3) species diversification through varied crop sequences and associations involving at least three different crops.
techniques.when_useful: Where the farmer can retain residue as cover, has access to a direct-seeding drill, and plans crop sequences across seasons rather than a single crop.
techniques.benefits: FAO states that conservation agriculture enhances biodiversity and natural biological processes, contributing to increased water and nutrient use efficiency and improved, sustained crop production.
techniques.limitations: All three principles work together: residue retention conflicts with residue removal or burning, and minimum disturbance needs suitable seeding equipment. FAO presents the system as a whole and does not claim a specific yield increase for a single component.
techniques.modern_relevance: It is the reference framework FAO uses for climate-smart cropping systems and soil-health programmes, and it is why cover crops, mulching and diversification appear in modern practice guidance.
techniques.crop_scope_note: FAO describes the system as general farming-system guidance and does not give crop-specific rates or seeding specifications.

regions.scope_note: FAO describes conservation agriculture as a farming system applicable across regions; local adaptation is required.

evidence.claim: Conservation agriculture rests on three principles — minimum mechanical soil disturbance, permanent soil organic cover of at least 30 percent, and species diversification with at least three crops.
evidence.source_section: Conservation Agriculture — three principles
evidence.note: Recorded as international guidance from FAO; not a field trial result for any one farm.

techniques.application_practice: Apply the three principles together: avoid tillage and place seed/fertilizer directly, keep at least 30 percent soil cover with residues or cover crops, and diversify with varied crop sequences and associations of at least three crops.
techniques.limitations: The three principles must be applied together to work as described by FAO; partial adoption is not what the source describes.

techniques.title: System of Rice Intensification (SRI)
techniques.summary: Rice establishment and water-management method documented by ICAR's Directorate of Water Management (Bhubaneswar, Odisha): young single seedlings, wider square spacing and unflooded, intermittently dried soil.
techniques.overview: SRI is a set of rice-management practices: very young seedlings planted singly and widely in a square pattern, and a soil-water regime that keeps the field unflooded with intermittent drying instead of continuous flooding.
techniques.principle: The method changes the plant's growing environment rather than the variety: young seedlings transplanted singly establish with less root disturbance, wide square spacing gives each plant more soil volume, light and air, and keeping the field unflooded with intermittent irrigation keeps oxygen available to the roots and soil organisms.
techniques.method_practice: The ICAR bulletin describes: 10-15 day old seedlings with about three leaves; transplanting a single seedling per hill; wider spacing in a square pattern; and intermittent irrigation with alternate wetting and drying instead of keeping the field continuously flooded.
techniques.when_useful: In irrigated rice where the farmer can control water and can transplant young seedlings carefully — the bulletin is based on work at Bhubaneswar, Odisha, and reports the method with water-saving irrigation.
techniques.benefits: The bulletin presents SRI with alternate wetting and drying as a water-saving approach for rice that maintains crop performance while using less irrigation water; it also documents reduced plant densities and unflooded fields as part of the method.
techniques.limitations: The method needs precise nursery management (young seedlings), careful transplanting, and water control for alternate wetting and drying; where irrigation cannot be controlled, the water regime cannot be followed. Outcomes depend on soil, season and management, so AGRIQ reports the bulletin's described method rather than a guaranteed result for a specific field.
techniques.modern_relevance: It is India's reference approach to water-saving rice establishment, and it is the documented basis for combining SRI with alternate wetting and drying in the eastern region.

regions.scope_note: ICAR bulletin published by the Directorate of Water Management, Bhubaneswar.
Research bulletin produced at Bhubaneswar, Odisha; local adaptation still required.

techniques.application_practice: Raise and transplant 10-15 day old seedlings singly at wider square spacing, and manage water by keeping the field unflooded with intermittent wetting and drying instead of continuous flooding.

techniques.title: Alternate wetting and drying (AWD) in rice
techniques.summary: Water-management practice for rice in which the field is allowed to dry intermittently between irrigations instead of remaining flooded throughout the season.
techniques.overview: Alternate wetting and drying means the rice field is not kept under continuous standing water. The soil is allowed to dry intermittently during the crop's growth and is then wetted again by irrigation or rain.
techniques.principle: Roots and soil organisms need oxygen. Allowing the soil surface to dry between wettings lets air back into the root zone, so the crop is grown with less total water than continuous flooding while the soil is re-wetted before the plant is stressed.
techniques.method_practice: The ICAR bulletin describes keeping fields unflooded and subjecting them to alternate wetting and drying, and documents SRI being combined with AWD water management.
techniques.when_useful: In irrigated rice where the farmer controls the water supply and can observe soil moisture between irrigations — the practice is described in an ICAR bulletin based at Bhubaneswar, Odisha.
techniques.benefits: The bulletin presents alternate wetting and drying as part of water-saving irrigation for rice, alongside SRI practices.
techniques.limitations: The safe drying point depends on soil type, crop stage and weather, and the bulletin's field scheduling cannot be transferred unchanged to another field. Without reliable water control or a way to observe soil moisture, the drying period cannot be judged. Where irrigation is uncertain, continuous flooding is what many farmers rely on.
techniques.modern_relevance: It is the core water-management technique of modern water-saving rice production and is reported together with SRI in eastern India.

regions.scope_note: Documented in an ICAR Directorate of Water Management bulletin published at Bhubaneswar.
Field work described for the Bhubaneswar region; local soils and water supply differ.

evidence.claim: Rice can be grown without continuous flooding by allowing the soil to dry intermittently (alternate wetting and drying), including together with SRI practices.
evidence.source_section: The Science behind the System of Rice Intensification — water management sections
evidence.note: ICAR research bulletin cited by publication.

techniques.application_practice: Irrigate, then let the soil surface dry intermittently before the next wetting instead of maintaining continuous standing water; re-wet before the crop shows water stress.
techniques.safety_precautions: Do not extend the drying period beyond what the soil and crop stage can take; where the water supply is unreliable, treat continuous flooding as the fallback rather than risking crop loss.

techniques.title: Drip irrigation (localized irrigation)
techniques.summary: Water dripped directly above the root zone instead of flooding or sprinkling the whole field, described by FAO as localized irrigation with maximized water efficiency.
techniques.overview: Drip irrigation delivers water as drops to the soil above the root zone only. FAO groups it with underground irrigation as localized irrigation, whose water efficiency is maximized because water is applied only where it is needed.
techniques.principle: Because water is placed at the root zone and not over the whole field, losses to runoff, deep percolation and evaporation from wet foliage are reduced; FAO also notes that the method does not bring water into contact with the foliage.
techniques.method_practice: Water is applied frequently in small amounts through emitters at the root zone. FAO describes localized irrigation as the family of systems that apply water directly and frequently to the roots, and links their spread to the availability of cheap plastic pipe from the 1970s.
techniques.when_useful: Where water is scarce or costly, and for crops whose value justifies the equipment. Because the foliage stays dry, FAO notes localized systems can be used with brackish water for crops that are not too sensitive to salinity.
techniques.benefits: FAO describes drip irrigation as maximizing water efficiency by applying water only where needed, and notes that water-saving technologies such as drip can also increase yields and reduce the rate of salinization.
techniques.limitations: It is a capital-intensive system that needs maintenance of emitters and filters, and its adoption depends on incentives and water pricing (FAO). Emitters can clog and the system must be designed for the field and crop; the source gives no design or scheduling rate.
techniques.modern_relevance: Localized irrigation is the modern successor of buried porous-jar irrigation and is the reference technology for water-saving crop production.
techniques.crop_scope_note: FAO describes localized irrigation as a system applicable across crops and regions; it does not give a per-crop design or irrigation schedule.

regions.scope_note: FAO describes the technology worldwide; design must be adapted to the field and water source.

evidence.claim: Drip irrigation is localized irrigation: water is applied only above the root zone, maximizing water efficiency, and water-saving technologies of this kind can also increase yields and reduce salinization.
evidence.source_section: Crops and Drops — localized irrigation systems
evidence.note: International guidance from FAO; the source states no design rate for a specific crop.

techniques.application_status_note: The FAO source explains the technology and its advantages but gives no design, emitter spacing or irrigation schedule, so AGRIQ states none. A drip design must come from a supplier and local extension service.
techniques.safety_precautions: Because the practice involves an engineered system, any installation should follow the equipment supplier's design and the local irrigation authority's guidance, not a general description.

techniques.title: Neem kernel aqueous extract (NKAE)
techniques.summary: Botanical preparation made by soaking ground neem kernels in water and spraying the filtered extract — with the university's documented preparation steps, spraying rate and timing.
techniques.overview: Neem kernel aqueous extract (NKAE) is a water extract of ground neem seed kernels used as a botanical spray. Azadirachtin, the main neem compound, acts on insects' growth and feeding rather than only killing them on contact.
techniques.principle: The extract contains limonoids (azadirachtin, salanin, meliantriol, nimbin). The source states that these compounds work on the insect's hormonal system rather than on the digestive or nervous system and lists the resulting effects: disrupting or inhibiting egg, larval or pupal development, blocking moulting, disrupting mating, repelling larvae and adults, deterring egg-laying, sterilising adults, poisoning larvae and adults, deterring feeding and inhibiting chitin formation.
techniques.traditional_purpose: To protect crops with farm-and-market-available neem material instead of chemical insecticides, and to reduce reliance on imported pesticides that the source links to resistance and resurgence problems.
techniques.method_practice: Dried neem seed is decorticated and winnowed, the clean kernels are ground to a fine powder (without pressing oil out), soaked in water, stirred with a pH-neutral adjuvant, left overnight and filtered; the residue is extracted again and used as manure.
techniques.preparation_instructions: Documented by the source: (1) take dried neem seed and remove the seed coat with a mortar and pestle or a mechanical decorticator; clean the kernel by winnowing off the seed coat. (2) Weigh 1 kg of clean neem kernel and grind it to the texture of fine tea powder, pounding in such a way that no oil comes out. (3) Soak the powder in about 10 litres of clean water, add 10 ml of a pH-neutral adjuvant (emulsifier/spreader mixture) and stir. (4) Keep the mixture overnight and filter it the next day through clean muslin cloth. (5) Add water to the residue and repeat the extraction 2-3 times; use the residue as manure for plants.
techniques.application_practice: Spray 1.25% to 5% NKAE (neem kernel weight basis). The source recommends the lower concentration as preventive and up to 5% as protective. Use the spray solution on the same day it is prepared; spray in low sunlight, preferably in the afternoon; ensure the whole plant foliage is covered. The source states the effect lasts 7-10 days.
techniques.when_useful: When a botanical spray is wanted and the field has white fly, bollworms, thrips, stem borer, brown plant hopper or leaf folder pressure — the registered-use list links those pests to neem-based azadirachtin products (see the azadirachtin record in the pesticide section for the regulated product data).
techniques.benefits: The source states that neem compounds act on insect growth and feeding and that it is the azadirachtin content that produces most of the effect; it presents neem as a botanical alternative to chemical insecticides and notes that the neem cake/residue can be used as manure.
techniques.limitations: The source states that neem extracts repel and disrupt growth rather than killing immediately, so the effect is slower than a fast-acting contact insecticide, and it lasts 7-10 days. The preparation must be used fresh on the day it is made. Preparation quality depends on the azadirachtin content of the seed lot and correct decortication and grinding.
techniques.safety_precautions: The source prescribes using the spray solution on the same day and spraying in low sunlight. AGRIQ adds no dosage beyond the source. As with any spray: wear gloves and cover nose and mouth, do not eat or smoke during spraying, and wash after spraying. Wash sprayed produce before consumption.
techniques.modern_relevance: Azadirachtin-based products are registered bio-insecticides in India (see the DPPQS 'Major Uses of Pesticides' bio-insecticide list). NKAE is the farm-prepared version of the same botanical principle.
techniques.crop_scope_note: The source states NKAE is recommended on crops generally and gives a concentration range; it does not name a specific crop or a per-crop rate.

regions.scope_note: University extension material; neem is widely available in India.

evidence.claim: NKAE preparation: 1 kg cleaned, finely ground neem kernel soaked in about 10 litres of water with 10 ml pH-neutral adjuvant, kept overnight, filtered, extraction repeated 2-3 times.
evidence.source_section: Neem Kernel Aqueous Extract
evidence.note: Preparation steps reproduced from the university extension source because it documents them; AGRIQ invents no recipe.

evidence.claim: Spraying 1.25% to 5% NKAE is recommended, preventive at the lower concentration and protective up to 5%; spray the same day, in low sunlight, effect lasting 7-10 days.
evidence.source_section: Spraying of NKAE
evidence.note: Rate and timing taken verbatim in substance from the source.

techniques.title: Neem leaf extract
techniques.summary: Water extract of green neem leaves used against leaf-eating caterpillars, grubs, locusts and grasshoppers, mainly in nurseries and kitchen gardens.
techniques.overview: A simpler neem preparation than NKAE: green neem leaves are soaked overnight in water, then ground and filtered, and the liquid is used as a botanical spray.
techniques.principle: As with other neem preparations, the leaf extract carries neem's limonoid compounds, which affect insect feeding and growth.
techniques.method_practice: Soak 1 kg of green neem leaves per 5 litres of water overnight; the next day grind the leaves and filter the extract.
techniques.preparation_instructions: Documented by the source: for 5 litres of water, 1 kg of green neem leaf is required. The leaves are soaked overnight in water, then ground the next day and the extract is filtered.
techniques.application_practice: Use the filtered extract against leaf-eating caterpillars, grubs, locusts and grasshoppers. The source notes the quantity of leaves needed for field-scale use is very high (about 80 kg per hectare) and therefore recommends this extract for nurseries and kitchen gardens.
techniques.when_useful: In nurseries and kitchen gardens where a small quantity is needed and green neem leaf is at hand, against leaf-eating caterpillars, grubs, locusts and grasshoppers.
techniques.benefits: Uses locally available green leaf material and needs no seed processing; the source presents it as useful for small-scale situations.
techniques.limitations: The leaf requirement is very high for field use (about 80 kg per hectare according to the source), so it is not practical for large areas. The source does not state a shelf life, a concentration for spraying or a per-crop rate for the leaf extract.
techniques.safety_precautions: Use the extract as prepared and avoid spraying in strong sunlight; standard spray safety applies (gloves, cover nose and mouth, wash after spraying). Wash produce before consumption.
techniques.crop_scope_note: The source names the nursery/kitchen-garden situation and the pest groups, not a field crop rate.

regions.scope_note: University extension material; neem is widely available in India.

techniques.title: Integrated Pest Management (IPM)
techniques.summary: Framework that combines biological, chemical, physical and crop-specific (cultural) measures, allowing pesticide use only when justified, to grow healthy crops with the least disruption to the agro-ecosystem.
techniques.overview: IPM is the careful consideration of all available pest-control techniques and the subsequent integration of appropriate measures that discourage pest populations from developing. It grew out of the pest-control crises caused by increasing pesticide use: secondary pest outbreaks, resurgence and resistance.
techniques.principle: IPM uses an ecological systems approach: it builds on ecosystem services such as pest predation while protecting others such as pollination, and encourages natural pest-control mechanisms instead of replacing them with routine spraying.
techniques.method_practice: Decisions are made field by field from monitoring: cultural, physical, biological and — only when justified — chemical measures are combined, and the full range of available options is considered against economic, environmental and social conditions.
techniques.when_useful: Whenever a crop needs protection: IPM is presented as the overall approach in which specific practices (cultural control, biological control, botanicals, and targeted chemistry) are combined rather than used alone.
techniques.benefits: FAO states that IPM reduces pesticide residues in food, feed, fibre and the environment, enhances ecosystem services such as pollination and healthy soils, increases income by lowering production costs and improving crop quality, and strengthens farmer knowledge and stewardship.
techniques.limitations: IPM requires monitoring, thresholds and knowledge of the local agro-ecosystem; it is a decision framework, not a product, so it gives no single prescription. Where monitoring is not done, IPM is reduced to its individual measures and loses the effect FAO describes.
techniques.modern_relevance: It is the framework FAO and Indian national programmes use to reduce pesticide risk, and it is why the modern pesticide records in AGRIQ are stored as approved-use information rather than as blanket recommendations.
techniques.crop_scope_note: FAO describes IPM as a framework for all crops and regions; it gives no crop-specific measure or rate.

regions.scope_note: FAO framework; measures must be chosen for the local crop and agro-ecosystem.

evidence.claim: IPM combines biological, chemical, physical and crop-specific (cultural) strategies to grow healthy crops and minimise pesticide use.
evidence.source_section: Integrated Pest Management — definition and role in sustainable agriculture
evidence.note: International framework guidance from FAO.

techniques.application_practice: Monitor the crop, identify the pest, and combine cultural, physical and biological measures; use chemical control only when the other measures are not enough, following the product label.
techniques.safety_precautions: Because IPM allows targeted chemical use, every chemical application still follows the official product label, the pre-harvest interval on that label, and the safety instructions in AGRIQ's pesticide information section.

pesticides.title: Safe use of pesticides — official DPPQS instructions (purchasing, storage, handling, spraying, disposal, first aid)
pesticides.mode_of_action: Not applicable: this record is not a product. It carries the official instructions that apply to any registered pesticide.
pesticides.approved_use: Applies to every registered pesticide. Official rules of the record: purchase only from a licensed dealer, only the quantity needed for one operation, only containers with an approved label showing batch number, registration number and manufacture/expiry date; never buy from unlicensed sellers, in bulk for a whole season, or with leaking/unsealed containers.
pesticides.label_directions_reference: Directorate of Plant Protection, Quarantine and Storage — Instruction for Safe Use of Pesticide: https://ppqs.gov.in/divisions/integrated-pest-management/instruction-safe-use-pesticide
pesticides.ppe: Official instruction: use protective clothing — hand gloves, face mask, cap, apron, full trousers — covering the whole body, and protect nose, eyes, ears and hands from spray spill. Never prepare spray solution without protective clothing. Do not eat, drink, smoke or chew during the whole operation. Never enter a treated field immediately after spraying without protective clothing.
pesticides.resistance_management: Official instruction: apply only the recommended dose and dilution, and never apply over-dose or higher concentrations than recommended; do not use left-over spray solution after 24 hours.
pesticides.environmental_precautions: Official instruction: spray in the wind direction, never against it; do not spray on a hot sunny day or in strong wind; do not spray just before or immediately after rain; left-over spray solution is to be disposed of at a safe place such as an isolated barren area and must not be drained into or near ponds or water lines; used/empty containers are to be crushed with a stone or stick and buried deep in soil away from water sources, and must never be reused for storing other articles.
pesticides.storage_handling: Official instruction: store pesticides away from the house premises, in their original containers, with insecticides and weedicides stored separately, the storage area marked with warning signs, and out of the reach of children and livestock; protect the storage from direct sunlight and rain and never transfer pesticides to another container.
pesticides.regulatory_status: Issued by the Directorate of Plant Protection, Quarantine and Storage under the Insecticides Act, 1968 framework; the official instruction to always follow the approved label and the recommended dose. AGRIQ does not replace the label: read the container label before use and take the container to a doctor in case of poisoning.
pesticides.first_aid_note: Official instruction: wash hands and face with clean water and soap before eating or smoking; if poisoning symptoms are observed, give first aid and show the patient to a doctor, and show the empty container to the doctor.

evidence.claim: Purchasing, storage, handling, spray-preparation, application and disposal rules for pesticides, including protective clothing, no over-dose, spraying with the wind, not before/after rain, container disposal and first-aid instructions.
